title: Episode 44: Buffalo Bill Cody and the Birth of the Wild West Show
description:
In 1882, in North Platte, Nebraska, legendary frontier scout William F. 'Buffalo Bill' Cody organized the 'Old Glory Blowout'—the world's first modern rodeo and the birth of 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West.' Touring the globe for thirty years with real Lakota warriors, Annie Oakley, and charging stagecoaches, Cody created the enduring international myth of the American West.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. When people around the world think of the American West, they picture charging stagecoaches, bucking broncos, sharpshooters, and grand cavalry charges. But that vivid, romantic mythology was not created by Hollywood; it was invented by a single, larger-than-life frontier showman: William Frederick Cody, universally known as 'Buffalo Bill.' An authentic frontier scout, buffalo hunter, and Medal of Honor recipient, Cody transformed his own real-life adventures into the greatest live touring theatrical spectacle the world had ever seen. In eighteen eighty-two, in the railroad town of North Platte, Nebraska, Cody organized a Fourth of July celebration that gave birth to Buffalo Bill's Wild West. For thirty years, he toured America and Europe, performing before Queen Victoria, the Pope, and millions of enchanted fans, defining the American frontier for all of human history. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE REAL FRONTIER SCOUT
Before he was an international showman who dined with kings and emperors, William Frederick Cody was the genuine article: an authentic, battle-tested legend of the untamed American frontier. Born in Scott County, Iowa Territory, in eighteen forty-six, Cody was orphaned at age eleven and immediately went to work as an ox-team messenger across the Great Plains to support his mother and sisters. At fourteen, he became one of the youngest riders for the legendary Pony Express, riding fifteen miles an hour through hostile territory; during the Civil War, he served as an elite scout for the Union cavalry; and in eighteen sixty-seven, he was hired by the Kansas Pacific Railroad to supply fresh buffalo meat to railway construction crews. Riding his bareback horse Brigham and armed with a fifty-caliber Springfield rifle he nicknamed 'Lucretia Borgia,' Cody killed four thousand two hundred and eighty buffalo in eighteen months, winning an epic eight-hour hunting contest against hunter Billy Comstock to claim the undisputed title of 'Buffalo Bill.' Appointed chief of civilian scouts for the Fifth United States Cavalry, Cody fought in sixteen Indian Wars battles, earning the Congressional Medal of Honor for gallantry in eighteen seventy-two. Tall, handsome, with flowing shoulder-length chestnut curls, a trim goatee, and extraordinary equestrian grace, Cody was a living dime-novel hero before he had even turned thirty. Cody had served as a Pony Express rider, Civil War scout, and buffalo hunter for the Kansas Pacific Railroad, winning the Congressional Medal of Honor for gallantry in action. Cody developed a deep respect for Native cultures, insisting that Indian performers in his show be paid equal wages and treated with personal dignity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE OLD GLORY BLOWOUT IN NORTH PLATTE
The birth of the modern Western show took place in North Platte, Nebraska, in the summer of eighteen eighty-two. Cody had established a magnificent home named Scout's Rest Ranch outside town, where he bred thoroughbred racehorses and prize Hereford cattle. When local civic leaders realized that North Platte had planned no community festivities for the upcoming Fourth of July, they pleaded with Cody to organize an entertainment. Cody conceived an audacious idea: rather than a standard patriotic parade or dull political speeches, he would organize an authentic, competitive exhibition of real frontier cowboy skills. Cody placed advertisements in newspapers across the prairie offering cash prizes for the fastest bronco riding, rope handling, and trick shooting, christening the event the 'Old Glory Blowout.' Cody expected a few dozen participants, but on July fourth, eighteen eighty-two, an astonishing crowd of five thousand cowboys, homesteaders, and Native Americans flooded into North Platte. Working cowboys competed in wild steer riding, lassoed wild buffalo, and reenacted a thrilling stagecoach defense. The thunderous, roaring success of the Old Glory Blowout proved to Cody that while the physical frontier was rapidly vanishing under barbed wire and rails, the entire world possessed an insatiable hunger to see the heroic spirit of the West brought to life. In eighteen eighty-two, Cody organized the Old Glory Blowout in North Platte, Nebraska, staging steer roping, bronco riding, and sharp-shooting contests that drew thousands of spectators from across the prairie. Frontier marksmen and trick riders practiced their feats daily, ensuring that audiences experienced an authentic, electrifying spectacle of western courage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BIRTH OF THE TRAVELING WILD WEST
In eighteen eighty-three, partnering with veteran theater manager Nate Salsbury, Cody created 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West.' Cody adamantly refused to permit the press to call it a 'show' or a 'circus'; he insisted it was an educational historical exhibition that preserved authentic Western life before it disappeared forever. The scale of the production was staggering: Cody mobilized an army of over two hundred real working cowboys, Mexican vaqueros, sharpshooters, and a herd of twenty live American bison, elk, and longhorn cattle. Traveling across the continent on a dedicated twenty-five-car private train, the company erected an immense outdoor arena covered by canvas grandstands that seated twenty thousand spectators. The performances were thrilling, sensory masterworks: a genuine Deadwood stagecoach rattled across the arena under attack by whooping riders, rescued at the last second by Buffalo Bill galloping in on his white horse, Duke, firing blank cartridges from his Winchester rifle, surrounded by thundering hooves, pungent black powder smoke, and the stirring music of the Cowboy Band. The traveling Wild West show featured authentic Concord stagecoaches, living bison herds, Pawnee and Lakota warriors, and hundreds of authentic frontier cowboys recreating historical battles.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: LITTLE SURE SHOT: ANNIE OAKLEY
In eighteen eighty-five, Cody made the most brilliant promotional decision of his career by hiring a five-foot-tall, twenty-four-year-old Ohio farm girl named Phoebe Ann Moses: known to the world as 'Annie Oakley.' Billed as 'Little Sure Shot'—a nickname bestowed upon her by Chief Sitting Bull—Annie Oakley was an astonishing prodigy with a rifle and shotgun. Modest, sweet, and impeccably dressed in modest calf-length skirts she sewed herself, Annie stepped into the arena and performed shooting feats that defied human comprehension: shooting the ashes off a cigarette held in her husband's lips at thirty paces, splitting playing cards edge-on at forty feet, and tossing glass balls into the air, spinning around, and blasting them to dust before they hit the ground. Annie Oakley shattered Victorian stereotypes of delicate femininity, proving that a woman could out-shoot any man on Earth while maintaining impeccable grace, becoming the show's beloved, shining star for sixteen years. Annie Oakley joined the show as Little Sure Shot, astonishing audiences by shooting the ash off cigarettes held in her husband lips and splitting playing cards edgewise at thirty paces.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: CHIEF SITTING BULL JOINS THE TROUPE
Even more remarkable was Cody's recruitment of the supreme spiritual leader of the Lakota Sioux: Chief Sitting Bull. Just nine years after Custer's defeat at the Little Bighorn, Sitting Bull was living on the Standing Rock reservation under military surveillance. Cody used his personal influence with the War Department to secure permission for Sitting Bull to tour with the Wild West in eighteen eighty-five. When Sitting Bull walked into the arena wrapped in a traditional buffalo robe, holding his eagle-feather warbonnet, crowds greeted him with awe and respect. Cody treated Sitting Bull with absolute dignity, paying him fifty dollars a week, giving him exclusive rights to sell autographed photographs, and presenting him with a gray performing horse that bowed on command. Sitting Bull used his earnings to distribute money to destitute newsboys and homeless children on street corners in New York and Montreal. When Sitting Bull departed the show, he presented Cody with a cherished sacred peace pipe, cementing an extraordinary friendship between the former battlefield enemies. Chief Sitting Bull toured with Cody throughout the summer of eighteen eighty-five, greeted by cheering crowds in every major city across the United States and Canada.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: CONQUERING EUROPEAN ROYALTY
In eighteen eighty-seven, Cody took his colossal spectacle across the Atlantic for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee in London, and the result was an unprecedented cultural triumph. Over two and a half million Britons packed into the arena at Earl's Court. Queen Victoria, who had lived in deep seclusion since the death of Prince Albert twenty-six years earlier, made an unprecedented public appearance to attend the show. When the American flag was carried into the arena, the Queen of the British Empire rose to her feet and bowed—the first time a British monarch had ever saluted the Stars and Stripes. During a special command performance, the Prince of Wales, along with the kings of Greece, Belgium, Denmark, and Saxony, climbed inside the Deadwood stagecoach as Buffalo Bill galloped alongside, defending the royal passengers from a mock Indian attack. Cody toured Europe for years, performing in Paris beneath the newly built Eiffel Tower, in Rome before Pope Leo the Thirteenth, and across Germany, transforming the American cowboy into an immortal international archetype. Cody took the extravaganza to England in eighteen eighty-seven for Queen Victoria Golden Jubilee, performing before royal heads of state who rode inside the Deadwood stagecoach during simulated Indian attacks.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE IMMORTAL MYTHMAKER
By the turn of the twentieth century, Buffalo Bill Cody was arguably the most famous and widely recognized human being on the planet. He was a visionary who advocated for women's voting rights, equal pay for female performers, and fair treatment of Native Americans at a time when such views were deeply unpopular. Although bad investments and financial panics cost him his fortune in his final years, Cody continued to mount his horse and tip his white Stetson hat to roaring audiences until his death in Denver in nineteen seventeen at the age of seventy. He was buried atop Lookout Mountain, overlooking the Great Plains he loved so dearly. Buffalo Bill did not merely show the West to the world; he invented its eternal soul—creating a timeless realm of freedom, courage, and frontier adventure that will ride on forever in the human imagination.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West proved that the frontier was more than a geographical place; it was an enduring spirit of human daring that captured the heart of the world. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we continue our weekly journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until then, stay curious.
